The order is fixed — label, then value, then traits, then hint — and the hint is the only part the user can silence, under Settings › Accessibility › VoiceOver › Verbosity › Speak Hints.

- **label** is what the element is: short, capitalised, no trailing period, and never the word "button" — the trait already says that. It is user-facing copy, so it goes through the same localisation as the visible text.
- **value** is what it reads right now: "On", "4 stars", "60 percent", the text inside a field. Anything that changes while the label stays the same belongs here, because VoiceOver re-reads the value of the focused element on its own.
- **traits** change behaviour, not just wording. `.isButton` makes a double tap activate it, `.isHeader` puts it on the rotor's Headings list, and `.updatesFrequently`, `.isSelected` and `.isLink` each tell VoiceOver something it cannot see. In UIKit they are an option set on `accessibilityTraits`.
- **hint** is what will happen if you activate it — "Saves the article to your list" — spoken last, after a pause, and only when Speak Hints is on.

The trap is folding state into the label. `"Favourite button, on"` makes VoiceOver re-read the whole phrase on every toggle, hands the rotor and a braille display the wrong string, and says "button" twice. Split it: label "Favourite", value "On".

The second trap is a hint that carries something the user needs. Experienced VoiceOver users turn hints off first, so information parked in one is invisible to exactly the people who depend on the feature most.

The model to keep: label is what it is, value is what it says now, trait is what it does, hint is what will happen — and the screen still has to work with the hint missing.

`.accessibilityElement(children: .combine)` promotes the container to a single element and folds its children's labels into one; in UIKit the same move is `isAccessibilityElement = true` on the container, because the children of an accessibility element are never traversed.

- `.combine` merges the children's labels, values and traits in traversal order — the right choice for a card that behaves as one tappable thing.
- `.contain` keeps the children reachable as separate elements but marks the container as a group, so the rotor and VoiceOver's container gestures treat the card as a unit.
- `.ignore`, which is what a bare `.accessibilityElement()` does, drops the children entirely and expects you to supply the label yourself.

Combining costs you the children's swipe stops: the heart button is no longer an element of its own, so the only place its action can live is the Actions rotor — name it yourself with `.accessibilityAction(named: "Save")` instead of trusting the merge to label it well. One destination plus one or two extra actions is exactly the shape this is for. A card holding three genuinely independent controls should stay as separate elements.

Two things bite. Decorative subviews are merged too, so an image with an inferred label and a badge shape land inside the combined sentence — mark them `.accessibilityHidden(true)` first. And a combined element cannot be skimmed: forty words of body copy in one stop is worse than five stops, because there is no way to move around inside it.

The rule of thumb: one element per thing the user can act on. Five stops each reading a fragment is noise; one stop that reads like a sentence, with the extra actions on the rotor, is the target.

In UIKit you hand the container an ordered `accessibilityElements` array; in SwiftUI there is no array to set, so you group with `.accessibilityElement(children: .contain)` and reorder the siblings inside with `.accessibilitySortPriority`.

- The defaults differ. UIKit derives the order geometrically from the subviews' frames within a container, respecting the layout direction. SwiftUI derives it from the declaration order of the view tree. Both are correct until you use a `ZStack`, an `.overlay`, an `.offset` or absolute positioning — that is where the drawn position and the source order stop agreeing.
- `accessibilityElements: [Any]?` replaces the automatic ordering completely, so anything you leave out of the array disappears from VoiceOver entirely. It is a stored array, not a computation, so rebuild it whenever the subviews change.
- `.accessibilitySortPriority(_:)` sorts siblings inside one container, higher first, default `0`. It cannot move an element between containers: if two views sit in different groups, no priority will interleave them, and that is the usual reason "the modifier does nothing".
- A view that is visually behind something must leave the tree, not just be covered. Use `.accessibilityHidden(true)`, or `.accessibilityAddTraits(.isModal)` in SwiftUI and `accessibilityViewIsModal = true` in UIKit on a custom overlay so everything behind it is skipped.

The order should match how a sighted person reads the screen — not the z-order, and not the order the subviews happened to be added in. Check it by swiping right through the screen once with VoiceOver on: if the sequence surprises you, it will surprise everybody.

Anything a gesture does must also exist as a named action — `.accessibilityAction(named:)` in SwiftUI, `accessibilityCustomActions` in UIKit — and a control with a range becomes adjustable so the up and down swipes drive it.

### The Actions rotor
- Named actions land on VoiceOver's Actions rotor: the user rotates to Actions, flicks up or down to pick one, then double-taps. Switch Control and Full Keyboard Access read the same list, so one implementation serves three input methods.
- `List`'s own `swipeActions` and a `contextMenu` are exposed automatically. You write custom actions for gestures you invented — a long-press menu, a drag handle, a two-finger pan.
- Two system actions are worth wiring by hand: `.accessibilityAction(.escape)` for the two-finger scrub that should dismiss a custom sheet, and `.accessibilityAction(.magicTap)` for the one thing the screen exists to do — answer the call, start the timer.

### Adjustable elements
- `.accessibilityAdjustableAction { direction in ... }` supplies the adjustable trait itself, so the vertical swipes become increment and decrement. UIKit needs `accessibilityTraits.insert(.adjustable)` plus overrides of `accessibilityIncrement()` and `accessibilityDecrement()`.
- Keep `accessibilityValue` in step with the change and speak a unit — "3 of 5", "60 percent" — never a bare number.

The failure mode is a slider built on a pan gesture with no adjustable trait: VoiceOver has already bound that swipe to "next element", so the control is not merely awkward, it is unreachable. Name each action with a verb, keep the list to about five, and never let a gesture be the only way to do something.

It posted `.screenChanged`, which is a whole-screen context switch; a result message belongs in an `.announcement`, which speaks without moving focus.

`UIAccessibility.post(notification:argument:)` has four values you use in practice:

1. `.announcement` — speaks the string you pass and leaves focus alone. This is the one for a save confirmation, a toast, a background error.
2. `.layoutChanged` — part of the screen changed. Pass `nil` and VoiceOver re-reads the layout without moving; pass an element and focus moves there, which is right for a validation error the user must deal with now.
3. `.screenChanged` — a new context. It plays the page-turn sound and throws focus to the first element, discarding wherever the user was. Correct only when you swapped a whole screen yourself inside a custom container; wrong for anything smaller.
4. `.pageScrolled` — speaks a position string such as "page 3 of 10" for a custom paging view.

The other half of the problem is announcements being swallowed. VoiceOver drops a plain announcement if it is mid-sentence, which is why one posted right after a screen appears is never heard. Since iOS 17 you set the priority on an `AttributedString` — `accessibilitySpeechAnnouncementPriority` of `.high` interrupts, `.default` queues, `.low` is dropped if something else is speaking — and post it through `AccessibilityNotification.Announcement`.

The mental model: focus is the user's cursor. Move it only when the screen genuinely changed under them. And when the change is the user's own doing, often you post nothing at all — updating `accessibilityValue` on the focused element is enough, because VoiceOver re-reads it by itself.

The fixed height is the bug: let the text drive the height, scale the constants around it with `@ScaledMetric` or `UIFontMetrics`, and clamp only elements that genuinely cannot reflow.

### What scales, and what you have to scale yourself
- Dynamic Type has twelve sizes; the five accessibility ones sit past `.extraExtraExtraLarge`. Body runs 17 pt at the default `.large` to 53 pt at `.accessibility5`, while Large Title only goes 34 pt to 60 pt — the scale is non-linear on purpose, so the hierarchy compresses instead of multiplying.
- Text scales for free when the font is a text style: `.font(.body)` in SwiftUI, `.preferredFont(forTextStyle:)` with `adjustsFontForContentSizeCategory = true` in UIKit. `Font.custom(_:size:relativeTo:)` scales a brand font against a named style; `Font.custom(_:fixedSize:)` is the one font API that opts out entirely.
- Hard-coded numbers do not scale. `@ScaledMetric(relativeTo: .headline) private var avatar: CGFloat = 40` grows an avatar with the text, and `UIFontMetrics(forTextStyle:).scaledValue(for:)` is the UIKit equivalent for a constraint constant.
- Past `.accessibility1` you reflow rather than shrink: check `dynamicTypeSize.isAccessibilitySize` and swap an `HStack` for a `VStack` through `AnyLayout`, or let `ViewThatFits` choose.

### When clamping is defensible
`.dynamicTypeSize(...DynamicTypeSize.accessibility1)` caps a subtree, and `.dynamicTypeSize(.large)` pins it. That is fair for a chart axis, a dense numeric table or a decorative badge that has nowhere to grow. Clamping the whole app is not a fix — it is how you make the setting useless for the person who turned it on.

`.lineLimit(1)` with `.minimumScaleFactor(0.5)` looks like a solution and is a regression: it shrinks the text the user asked to enlarge. The habit that prevents all of this is `minHeight`, never `height`, around anything containing text.

Read `\.accessibilityReduceMotion` and replace the motion with a cross-fade — the system only strips its own animations, never yours, and three sibling settings work the same way.

- **Reduce Motion** — `\.accessibilityReduceMotion` / `UIAccessibility.isReduceMotionEnabled`. Honour it for parallax, spring and scale transitions, autoplaying video and looping animations. Replace them with a short opacity cross-fade rather than nothing: a jump cut is disorienting too. The separate "Prefer Cross-Fade Transitions" toggle is `UIAccessibility.prefersCrossFadeTransitions` if you drive your own push and pop.
- **Reduce Transparency** — `\.accessibilityReduceTransparency`. UIKit and SwiftUI make their own materials opaque for you; a hand-rolled `.blur()` or a translucent overlay is yours to swap for a solid colour.
- **Increase Contrast** — `\.colorSchemeContrast == .increased` / `UIAccessibility.isDarkerSystemColorsEnabled`. Asset-catalog colours can carry a High Contrast variant that is picked up automatically; hard-coded borders and secondary text need the branch written by hand.
- **Bold Text** — `\.legibilityWeight == .bold` / `UIAccessibility.isBoldTextEnabled`. System fonts embolden themselves; a custom family needs you to select the heavier face.

In UIKit you read the booleans and subscribe to the matching `UIAccessibility.…DidChangeNotification`, or use `registerForTraitChanges` for the contrast and legibility-weight traits. In SwiftUI they are environment values, so a change re-renders the view for free.

Test all four without leaving Xcode: the Accessibility Inspector's Settings pane flips them on the simulator, `xcrun simctl ui booted increase_contrast enabled` scripts them for a screenshot run, and previews take `.environment(\.accessibilityReduceMotion, true)`.

The rule: the system honours these for its own components. Every animation, blur and colour you wrote yourself is yours to check.

Both are static checks of one visible screen — missing labels, clipped text, small hit regions, contrast ratios — so neither has any opinion on whether the labels mean anything or whether the task can be completed.

### What the two tools do
- The Accessibility Inspector (Xcode › Open Developer Tool) has three panes that matter: inspection, which shows the label, value, traits and frame of whatever you point at; the audit, a one-shot check of the visible screen; and Settings, which flips Dynamic Type, Reduce Motion, Increase Contrast and Bold Text on the simulator.
- `XCUIApplication().performAccessibilityAudit()` runs the same checks inside a UI test and fails it. Narrow the run with `performAccessibilityAudit(for: [.dynamicType, .contrast, .hitRegion, .textClipped, .elementDetection, .sufficientElementDescription, .trait])`, and pass the closure form to suppress a known issue — returning `true` from the handler means you have dealt with it.

### What neither will ever catch
- A label that exists but is wrong: "Button", "image_23", or the raw SF Symbol name. The check is presence, not sense.
- Reading order, grouping, and whether a card is one swipe stop or five.
- A custom gesture with no matching `.accessibilityAction(named:)`.
- Focus after a sheet dismisses, and whether an announcement was ever spoken — audits see a frozen screen, not a sequence.
- Meaning carried only by colour, when the contrast ratio itself passes.

So wire the audit into CI as a regression net over every screen, and then do the part only a person can do: turn on VoiceOver, enable Screen Curtain with a three-finger triple tap, and complete a real task without looking. A screen can pass every automated check and still be impossible to buy anything on.

Colour is the only carrier of the meaning, so the status is invisible to a colour-blind user, to anyone with Differentiate Without Color on, and to VoiceOver entirely — the state has to be readable a second way.

### The contrast numbers, and how they get measured wrong
- WCAG asks for 4.5:1 on body text, 3:1 on text at 18 pt or 14 pt bold, and 3:1 on an icon or control that carries meaning. Apple's HIG uses the same 4.5:1 floor.
- Measure the resolved pair, not the asset: a dynamic colour resolves differently in dark mode and again under Increase Contrast. `UIColor.resolvedColor(with: traitCollection)` gives you the value actually drawn, and an asset catalog's High Contrast variant is what the system swaps in when `\.colorSchemeContrast` is `.increased`.
- The Accessibility Inspector's contrast check only understands text over a flat, opaque background. Text over a photo, a gradient or a `.ultraThinMaterial` is reported as passing and is the failure users actually hit.

### Carrying the meaning twice
- Red and green are the same dot to roughly 8% of men. Add a difference in shape — SF Symbols differ in silhouette, not only in tint — or a word, or a pattern.
- Read `\.accessibilityDifferentiateWithoutColor` (`UIAccessibility.shouldDifferentiateWithoutColor` in UIKit) and show the shape or the label unconditionally when it is on.
- VoiceOver never sees the tint at all: the state belongs in `accessibilityLabel` or `accessibilityValue`, and the dot itself should be `accessibilityHidden(true)`.

The test that costs nothing: screenshot the screen and desaturate it. If you can still tell paid from overdue, it passes; if you cannot, colour is doing work only some of your users can see.

A String Catalog is a build-time database: every build re-extracts the literals the compiler can see, merges them into the `.xcstrings` file, marks entries it can no longer find as stale rather than deleting them, and compiles the whole thing back down to per-language `.strings` and `.stringsdict` in the bundle.

### Reading the state column
- **NEW** — extracted, no translation yet; this is what a language's percentage counts.
- **NEEDS REVIEW** — the source-language string changed after the translation was made, so the old translation may no longer match. Xcode keeps it and asks you to confirm or replace it.
- **STALE** — the key was not found during this build's extraction. Usually dead code; sometimes a string you now build dynamically, so check before deleting.
- Keys you typed in by hand are `manual` and are never marked stale, and anything set to "Don't Translate" is skipped entirely.

### What extraction can and cannot see
- Literals only: `Text("Save")`, `String(localized:)`, `LocalizedStringResource`, `NSLocalizedString`, plus `InfoPlist.xcstrings` for permission prompts and the display name. `Text(viewModel.title)` produces no entry and silently ships the source language.
- Extraction needs `SWIFT_EMIT_LOC_STRINGS` ("Use Compiler to Extract Swift Strings"), on by default for new targets and often off in a project that predates catalogs.
- The `comment:` argument travels into the catalog and out into the XLIFF a translator opens through Product ▸ Export Localizations — without it they get a bare "Open" and no idea whether it is a verb.

What did not change is the runtime: lookup is still `<lang>.lproj/Localizable.strings`. The catalog replaced the editing format and absorbed `.stringsdict`, not the loading mechanism — which is why `Bundle.module` and table names work exactly as before.

Plural selection belongs to the language, not to your call site: the value picks a CLDR category and each language declares its own set, so the fix is a plural variation in the String Catalog rather than an `if count == 1`.

### How many forms you actually owe
- English has two categories (`one`, `other`), Russian four (`one`, `few`, `many`, `other`), Arabic and Welsh six, including `zero` and `two`. Japanese has one.
- Russian picks by the trailing digits, not the magnitude: 1, 21, 31 are `one`; 2–4 and 22–24 are `few`; 5–20 and 11–14 are `many`. No amount of `count == 1` reproduces that.
- The category is chosen from the formatted value, not the integer: in English `1.0` is `other`, so "1.0 items" is correct and "1.0 item" is not.
- English is already wrong today — `"\(count) items"` renders "1 items". The ternary that fixes English is what makes the bug untranslatable, because it hard-codes a two-form language into the call site.

### Writing it
- In the catalog, right-click the entry ▸ Vary by Plural, then fill only the categories that language has; Xcode compiles the variation into `.stringsdict`. Interpolating an `Int` gives the key `%lld items`, which is why the entry is named after the specifier and not after your Swift source.
- Two counts in one sentence means two substitutions, not two concatenated strings — word order is the translator's to choose, never yours.
- `^[\(count) item](inflect: true)` is automatic grammar agreement: it handles simple noun agreement for the languages Apple ships inflection rules for, but a plural variation is the portable answer.

CLDR gives English no `zero` category, so "No items" instead of "0 items" is a separate string you branch to in code — the catalog will not select it for you.

`Text` localizes only when its argument is a literal: a `String` variable binds to the non-localizing initializer, so the view model's title is rendered verbatim and was never extracted into the catalog — the fix is to store a `LocalizedStringResource` in the model instead of a `String`.

### The three types and what each is for
- `LocalizedStringKey` is what `Text("Save")`, `Button` and `Label` titles take. Interpolation becomes format specifiers, so `Text("\(n) items")` looks up `%lld items`. It resolves against `Bundle.main` at render time, which is why a literal inside a framework or SPM target needs `Text("Save", bundle: .module)`.
- `String(localized:table:bundle:comment:)` resolves now and hands you characters. Use it where you need a real `String`: an accessibility label you assemble by hand, a notification body, anything that is not a view.
- `LocalizedStringResource` is key + table + bundle + locale, resolved later. It is the right type for anything stored, sent across a process boundary or rendered by the system: model properties, App Intent titles, widget configuration. `Text(resource)` renders it.
- `NSLocalizedString` still works and is still extracted, but it has no Swift interpolation, so you pair it with `String(format:)` and lose the compiler's placeholder checking. New Swift code uses `String(localized:)`.

### Where it goes wrong
- `Text(model.title)` compiles, warns about nothing, and is invisible to extraction — no catalog entry, no missing-translation report, just English in the German build.
- Resolving early and caching freezes the language: a `static let` computed at launch survives a language change, a `LocalizedStringResource` does not.
- Use `Text(verbatim:)` deliberately for what must not be looked up — a username, a code, an already-formatted number.

Rule of thumb: a literal in a view stays a literal; a string you will show later or elsewhere is a `LocalizedStringResource`; a string you need characters from right now is `String(localized:)`.

The region does: `Locale.current` is the pair of settings, the language picks the words and the region picks every number, date, unit and calendar — so `en_DE` is English text with a 24-hour clock, a comma decimal separator and kilometres.

### Let the format styles decide
- `date.formatted(date: .abbreviated, time: .shortened)` takes field order, separators and hour cycle from the locale. A hand-written `dateFormat = "MM/dd/yyyy"` is wrong in every region but one; keep fixed patterns for machine data only, pinned to `Locale(identifier: "en_US_POSIX")` or `.iso8601`.
- The currency code belongs to the price, not to the user: `amount.formatted(.currency(code: order.currency))`. The locale chooses symbol placement and separators, it must never choose the currency, and you never convert.
- `Measurement(value: 5, unit: UnitLength.kilometers).formatted(.measurement(width: .abbreviated, usage: .road))` converts to miles for a US region. The conversion happens because you declared a `usage:`, not automatically.
- Names sort with `localizedStandardCompare`; `<` on `String` is a byte order that puts "Ä" after "Z".

### The traps
- Do not derive the region from `Locale.preferredLanguages.first` — that is the language list, and it disagrees with the region for exactly the user in the question.
- `Calendar.current` is not necessarily Gregorian (Thailand defaults to Buddhist), and `firstWeekday` is Sunday in the US, Monday in Germany, Saturday in much of the Gulf. A week grid built from a hardcoded Monday is broken before it renders.
- String interpolation of a `Double` always emits a dot: correct for JSON, wrong on screen.

Rule of thumb: anything a person reads goes through `.formatted(...)` with the current locale; anything a server reads goes through an explicitly fixed one.

Two independent systems are at work: mirroring is a layout decision you make per view, while the order of characters inside a line is decided by the Unicode bidirectional algorithm — and neither of them looks at your `leading` constraints.

### Characters and numerals
- A Latin run inside an Arabic sentence is reordered by the bidi algorithm, and neutral characters at its edges — `+`, `-`, `#`, brackets — attach to whichever side the algorithm decides, which is why "#A-1024" comes out inverted. Wrap a foreign run in an isolate, `\u{2068}` FSI … `\u{2069}` PDI, and it keeps its own direction inside the sentence.
- Never "fix" it by reversing the string. Storage order is already correct; only display order is mirrored, and a reversed string is corrupt everywhere else.
- Arabic locales may render digits as Arabic-Indic (`ar_EG` gives ١٢٣). `count.formatted()` follows the locale's numbering system; `"\(count)"` never does. When an identifier must stay Western, format it against `Locale(identifier: "ar-SA-u-nu-latn")`.

### Mirroring you have to decide
- A directional glyph opts in: `Image.flipsForRightToLeftLayoutDirection(true)`, or Direction ▸ Mirrors in the asset catalog, or `imageFlippedForRightToLeftLayoutDirection()` in UIKit.
- What must not flip: a brand mark, media transport, a clock face, a chart's time axis. UIKit has `semanticContentAttribute` set to `.playback`, `.spatial` or `.forceLeftToRight`; in SwiftUI you pin `.environment(\.layoutDirection, .leftToRight)` on that subtree.
- Read direction from the view, not the locale: `effectiveUserInterfaceLayoutDirection` and `@Environment(\.layoutDirection)` know about a forced subtree, `Locale.current` does not.
- Transforms do not mirror. `CGAffineTransform(translationX: 100, y: 0)` and a hardcoded `CGPoint` move right in both directions, so a hand-rolled swipe animation runs backwards.

Run the Right-to-Left Pseudolanguage before any Arabic exists: it mirrors the interface without translating, so layout bugs surface on their own instead of hiding behind unfamiliar text.

Run the app in Xcode's pseudolanguages: they expand, accent and bracket every localized string at load time, so truncation, concatenation and strings that were never extracted appear with no translator involved.

### What each pseudolanguage proves
- **Double-Length** repeats every string, which is a cheap stand-in for German and Finnish; anything with a fixed width or a single line clips immediately.
- **Accented** adds diacritics but keeps the text readable — anything still plain ASCII was never localized, which is exactly how you find a hardcoded literal or a string built by interpolation the extractor cannot see.
- **Bounded String** brackets each string, so a sentence assembled from two localized halves shows its seam.
- **Right-to-Left** mirrors the interface without translating anything.

### Turning it into a gate
- Scheme ▸ Run ▸ Options ▸ App Language picks one locally. For CI, `xcodebuild test -testLanguage de -testRegion DE`, or set the launch arguments yourself: `app.launchArguments += ["-AppleLanguages", "(ar)", "-AppleLocale", "ar_SA"]`.
- A text assertion will not catch truncation — a clipped label still reports its full string to accessibility. `try app.performAccessibilityAudit(for: [.textClipped, .dynamicType])` does: it fails the test when a label's text does not fit the frame it was given.
- Pair it with snapshot images of the screens that matter, taken at double length and the largest Dynamic Type. A diff is the only thing that catches a layout that overlaps or reflows badly rather than clipping.

What pseudolocalisation proves is your plumbing, not your translations. It will never catch a wrong plural rule, a mistranslated verb, or a term that reads as an insult in Portuguese — those need real strings and a native reader.

None of the three reads your catalog the way the UI does: the store listing lives in App Store Connect, a push is localized on the device through `loc-key`, and App Shortcut phrases have to sit in their own String Catalog.

### App Store Connect
- Name, subtitle, keywords, description, What's New, screenshots and previews are per-locale in App Store Connect — through the API or `fastlane deliver` if you automate it — and never in the bundle. A locale you leave empty falls back to your primary language.
- In-app purchase display names and subscription descriptions are localized there too. Prices come from the storefront: never format, convert or hardcode them in the app.

### Push notifications
- Send keys, not sentences: `title-loc-key`, `loc-key` and `loc-args` in the `alert` payload. The device looks them up in the installed app's compiled strings, so the banner is in the user's language and the server never has to know it.
- The key must exist in the version the user has installed. A key added this release renders as the raw key on an older build, so keys are additive and never renamed.
- `loc-args` substitute positionally, so the string needs `%1$@`-style specifiers if a translator is to reorder them. Anything needing real formatting — a date, a plural — belongs in a Notification Service Extension, which runs your code in the user's locale before the banner appears.

### Siri and Shortcuts
- App Intent titles and parameters are `LocalizedStringResource` and extract normally, but `AppShortcutsProvider` phrases do not: they must live in a separate catalog named `AppShortcuts.xcstrings`, and every phrase has to contain `\(.applicationName)`.
- Translating a phrase is authoring, not translation — each language needs several natural ways a person would actually say it.

The fourth one people forget is in the bundle after all: permission prompts and the display name, in `InfoPlist.xcstrings`.
